problem: SPL compares an agent's path length to the shortest path, ignoring the agent's dynamics. It therefore favors jerky point-turn behavior and penalizes agents that take smoother, faster curved paths. It also does not penalize redundant idle actions such as pausing or pivoting.
motivation: Real mobile robots (LoCoBot, TurtleBot, Fetch) have unicycle-like dynamics and can move and turn at the same time. The shortest path is not always the fastest, and point-turn policies transfer to real robots with jerky, slow, power-hungry motion. A metric conditioned on the agent's dynamics is needed to measure how well an agent exploits its embodiment.
key_idea: Replace the shortest-path baseline in SPL with the fastest possible completion time under the agent's dynamics (computed with a dynamics-aware RRT*-Unicycle planner), giving SCT = S * T / max(C, T).
insight: SPL and SCT rank agents differently. In sim, unicycle agents get lower SPL^∩ (~90 vs ~95) but much higher SCT^∩ (>88 vs ~72) than point-turn agents, because smooth curves lengthen paths but shorten time. Un-shaping the geodesic reward (decaying reward) improves the unicycle agents (U-6 SCT 82.15→88.92, success 93.16→98.79) but leaves the point-turn agent unchanged, because shortest and fastest paths coincide for point-turn dynamics. The gain from smoother motion is not an optimization of path length, so SPL would mislead here.
method: SCT metric: SCT = S·T/max(C,T), where C is the agent's completion time and T is the fastest possible time under the agent's dynamics (max linear 0.25 m/s, max angular 10°/s).

RRT*-Unicycle: RRT* over poses (x,y,θ). A new node's θ is left unset and determined by the fastest path from its best parent. Sampling is biased near the A* shortest path until a path is found, and near the current fastest path afterwards. Edges are costed by time.

Free-space fastest path: an optional initial in-place pivot, then a constant-curvature arc at max linear velocity. The pivot amount comes from a brute-force lookup table on relative heading and distance. Chained arcs approximate splines. Pose-to-pose rewiring cost adds a final pivot time.

Discrete velocity action spaces: Point-turn (4 actions), Unicycle-6 (2 linear × 3 angular) and Unicycle-15 (3 × 5), polled at 1 Hz. Backward motion is disallowed and stopping is a zero-velocity action.
Policy: DD-PPO with ResNet-50 depth encoder and a 2-layer LSTM (512 hidden) taking goal [r,cosθ,sinθ] and the previous action. Trained on 64 parallel workers for 150M steps.

Decaying reward: step reward -β·Δgeodesic - 0.01 with terminal reward 2.5·S (not SPL-scaled). β decays linearly from 1 to 0 over 80M steps, so the agent is eventually driven only by speed and success.

Real-world evaluation: LoCoBot with a D435 depth camera and LiDAR egomotion. Max angular velocity raised to 30°/s and sliding turned off in training. Fastest time is computed with RRT*-Unicycle on a Hector SLAM map, and shortest path with vanilla RRT*.

numbers_note: Table 1 also has SCT∩/SPL∩ metrics, recorded as SCT_cap/SPL_cap. The real-world Point-turn baseline had SCT 37.39, SPL 91.08, time 73.50 s.
results: Unicycle agents with the decaying reward reach SCT 88.92 (U-6) and 86.01 (U-15), against 65.99 for the best point-turn agent, while SPL is similar or lower. On the real LoCoBot, Unicycle-6 is faster than point-turn (47.83 s vs 73.50 s, about 35% faster), with SCT 56.98 vs 37.39 but SPL 89.16 vs 91.08.
limitations: Discrete action spaces represent only a subset of the dynamics, which prevents near-optimal SCT.
RRT*-Unicycle uses approximate arc-based free-space paths and an overestimated pose-to-pose cost, so T is only near-optimal, and the fastest time assumes specific max velocities.
The real-world evaluation is very small (2 episodes × 3 trials, 12 runs) in a single apartment.
